title: Who Counts as a Reader?
author: Simon Pollard
summary: Simon Pollard, drawing on four years of longlisting information books for the UKLA Book Awards, argues that schools undercount readers by recognising only the child curled up with a novel. Children who say they dislike reading are often devoted readers of information books, magazines, maps and manuals, and browsing and studying pictures count as reading. He shows how the twenty longlisted titles offer many entry points and a wide range of voices, using Rudine Sims Bishop's mirrors, windows and sliding doors. He adds that teachers who read widely are better placed to nurture readers unlike themselves. He closes with a practical proposal that trusts put good books in family hubs, libraries and school receptions, and a simple challenge to hand a reluctant reader an information book on something they love.
points: Many self-described non-readers are keen readers of non-fiction, and teachers risk missing them because they expect readers to look like novel lovers.
Information books supply varied hooks, from a book about bums that tells the story of evolution to a dyslexia-friendly biography, so any one could prompt a child to say 'I'm a reader'.
The longlist is read through Sims Bishop's mirrors, windows and sliding doors, and Pollard asks whose lives and expertise are on a school's shelves and whose are missing.
Research on reading for pleasure suggests teachers who read beyond their own tastes are better placed to notice and nurture readers unlike themselves.
Pollard turns the point into practice: trusts can put books where families already are and give pupils books of their own at transition, at little cost.
quotes: Many children who don’t see themselves as readers are devoted readers of information books. They pore over shark facts, football annuals, maps and manuals. Browsing, dipping in and studying the pictures all count as reading.
The child with A Natural History of Bums open on their knee, laughing and telling everyone nearby what they’ve just found out, may not be recognised as a reader at all.
When we only recognise one kind of reader, we misread the others.
Every one of those books might be the one that makes a child say, for the first time: I’m a reader.
Mirrors reflect children’s own lives back to them. Windows show them lives unlike their own. Sliding doors invite them to step inside. Information books can be all three.
the research on reading for pleasure keeps returning to the same point: teachers who read widely, beyond their own tastes, are better placed to notice and nurture readers who aren’t like them.
The next time a child tells you they don’t like reading, hand them an information book on something they love. Then see what happens.
